# Physical Effort Shifts the Decision Criterion in Older Adults {#sec-ch4}

```{r ch4-setup}
#| include: false
source(file.path("chapter4", "setup.R"), local = knitr::knit_global())
```

```{=latex}
\ucrsmalltablestrue
```

This chapter is in preparation for submission for publication as:

> Dastgheib, M., Bennett, I. J., & Seitz, A. R. (in prep.). Physical effort shifts the decision criterion in older adults.

This chapter analyzes data from the same participants as Chapter 3 and as @sun2026handgrip, a preprint co-first-authored by Andrew Y. Sun and Mohammad Dastgheib; inclusion criteria differ slightly by research question.

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Everyday decisions are often made while the body is working, yet little is known about how physical effort changes decision-making in older adults. Physical effort could degrade the quality of the evidence on which a decision is based, change how much evidence people require before committing to a response (response caution), or bias them toward one response. We tested these accounts in `r v("n_final")` older adults who judged whether two tones, or two visual gratings, were the same or different while squeezing a handgrip at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of their maximum force. Pupil size was recorded throughout. Choices and response times were analyzed with a hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion model, which separates evidence quality, response caution and the starting point, a bias toward one response set before the stimulus appears. High physical effort did not reduce evidence quality overall, and any additional cost on the hardest discriminations was small. Instead, it produced a small shift in the criterion against which evidence was evaluated toward "same" responses on every trial, which lowered accuracy when two similar stimuli differed. Response caution and the starting point were essentially unchanged. High physical effort enlarged the pupil only weakly during the grip, reliably in the auditory task alone. Larger pupil responses during a decision accompanied greater response caution on that trial, but pupil size measured before the decision did not predict caution. Physical effort therefore mainly changed the criterion older adults used to evaluate evidence, not the quality of that evidence.

## Introduction {#sec-ch4-1}

Many everyday decisions are made while the body is working, such as judging a gap in traffic while gripping a steering wheel or reading a label while carrying groceries. Combining a cognitive task with a motor task costs older adults more than younger adults [@Verhaeghen2003-ft], and sustained isometric force is one such motor demand: an effortful handgrip impairs cognitive control and working memory in later life [@Azer2023-ft]. Accuracy and response time (RT) show that performance suffers, but not which part of the decision process changes.

Chapter 2 [@Dastgheib2026-crpi] used the same 5% and 40% handgrip levels in younger adults performing a working-memory task and two discrimination tasks, one auditory and one visual. Harder trials were less accurate in every task and slower in both discrimination tasks, high physical effort slowed responses only in the visual discrimination task, and task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure. High physical effort also enlarged the pupil across the trial. In younger adults, physical effort and task difficulty therefore appeared to draw on separate resources. Chapter 3 then showed, in the present sample, that high physical effort lowered "different" responses without reducing sensitivity. On trials with identical stimuli the reduction was of similar size but uncertain on its own. Choices alone cannot tell whether this reflects a shifted criterion, a change in how much evidence participants required, or a bias set before the stimulus; separating these requires RTs. This chapter uses both to answer that question.

The drift-diffusion model decomposes choices and RTs into latent components [@Ratcliff2008-fj]. It treats a two-choice decision as noisy evidence that accumulates until it reaches one of two boundaries. Drift rate (*v*) is the average direction and speed of accumulation. Boundary separation (*a*) is how much evidence is required before responding, and so indexes response caution. The starting point (*z*) is where accumulation begins between the two boundaries: 0.5 is unbiased, and a value above 0.5 gives "different" a head start before the probe arrives. Non-decision time (*t*~0~) covers encoding and response execution. Lower accuracy can therefore arise from less informative evidence, from responding on less evidence, or from a bias toward the wrong response. In older adults, the most consistent age differences are wider boundaries and longer non-decision times, whereas drift is often similar to that of younger adults on simple perceptual tasks [@ratcliff2001aging; @Theisen2021-fn], and older adults set boundaries more conservatively than would maximize their reward rate [@Starns2010-iu]. Response caution is therefore a plausible target of physical effort in this age group, alongside evidence quality.

A capacity account holds that physical effort competes with the judgment for a limited pool of processing resources [@Kahneman1973-jw; @Wickens2008-pj]. On each trial, participants judged whether a probe matched a preceding standard. If holding a 40% grip draws on the resources needed for that comparison, the evidence should become less informative: trials with a different probe and trials with an identical one would become harder to tell apart, so drift on the two kinds of trials would move closer together. Because a shared limit should cost most where discrimination is hardest, this loss of evidence quality should be largest on the hardest trials, producing an interaction between physical effort and task difficulty.

A policy account holds instead that physical effort changes how participants use the evidence, not the evidence itself. Participants could require more evidence before responding, to protect accuracy, which would widen the boundaries. Alternatively, they could require less, to end each effortful trial sooner, which would narrow them. Physical effort could also bias responding toward "same" or "different." A bias set before the stimulus appears would move the starting point. A bias in how the evidence is evaluated would instead shift the drift criterion, the reference against which evidence counts as favoring one response [@Ratcliff2008-fj]. Such a shift moves drift toward one response on every trial, so it can lower accuracy on difficult trials with a different probe even when evidence quality is intact. Distinguishing the capacity and policy accounts therefore requires estimating the criterion and evidence quality separately.

Pupil size offers a trial-by-trial physiological measure relevant to both accounts. It increases with task difficulty [@Beatty1982-wg; @Van_der_Wel2018-ko] and with physical effort [@Zenon2014-ze], although older adults have smaller pupils and a narrower range of dilation than younger adults [@Winn1994-pi; @Piquado2010-eu]. In diffusion-model analyses, larger trial-wise pupil dilation has been related to wider boundaries in a reinforcement-learning task [@Cavanagh2014-eh] and to smaller choice biases across several decision tasks [@De_Gee2020-ls]. Pupil responses, however, also increase with decision uncertainty and RT [@Urai2017-aw], so a pupil–boundary association could arise simply because longer decisions produce larger pupil responses. To test whether pupil-linked arousal helps determine how cautious a decision will be, rather than simply growing with longer decisions, pupil size must therefore be measured before the decision begins or in a window that ends before the response.

We tested the capacity and policy accounts in older adults performing auditory and visual same–different tasks while holding a handgrip at 5% or 40% of their maximum force. A hierarchical Bayesian drift-diffusion model estimated the effect of physical effort on each decision component, and @tbl-ch4-predictions sets out what each account predicts for each model term. Two predictions separate the accounts most clearly. The physical effort × stimulus term, which measures evidence quality, should be negative under the capacity account and close to zero under the policy account. Accuracy on Identical trials should fall if evidence quality is lost, but rise if the criterion or the starting point shifts toward "same" (@fig-ch4-predictions). Trial-wise pupil measures were then added to the same model to test whether pupil size tracked the effect of physical effort, which decision component tracked the task-evoked pupil response, and whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation.

| Model term (high vs. low physical effort) | What it measures | Capacity account | Policy account |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Physical effort × stimulus | Evidence quality: how far drift on trials with a different probe lies from drift on Identical trials | Lower, most on Hard trials | Unchanged |
| Physical effort effect on drift | Drift criterion: a shift of drift toward one response on every trial | Unchanged | May shift toward "same" or "different" |
| Physical effort effect on boundary separation | Response caution | Unchanged | May widen (protect accuracy) or narrow (finish effortful trials sooner) |
| Physical effort effect on the starting point | Bias toward one response before the probe | Unchanged | May shift toward one response |

: Predictions of the capacity and policy accounts for each term of the diffusion model. @fig-ch4-predictions shows what the two decisive patterns imply for drift and accuracy. {#tbl-ch4-predictions tbl-colwidths="[26,32,20,22]"}

## Methods {#sec-ch4-2}

### Participants {#sec-ch4-2-1}

Community-dwelling adults aged 60–90 years were recruited around the University of California, Riverside. All were right-handed, had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and hearing, and had no contraindication for MRI, no current psychotropic medication, no neurological disorder and no major systemic condition (including diabetes). Of `r v("n_enrolled")` enrolled participants, `r nw(v("n_excluded"))` were excluded (suspected mild cognitive impairment; possible essential tremor). That left `r v("n_final")` older adults (@tbl-ch4-demographics). Choices and confidence in this cohort were analyzed by @sun2026handgrip and, at the level of trials, in Chapter 3. Under the inclusion criteria, `r v("n_adt") + v("n_vdt") - v("n_final")` participants contributed data to both tasks and `r nw(2 * v("n_final") - v("n_adt") - v("n_vdt"))` to only one (auditory, `r v("n_adt")`; visual, `r v("n_vdt")`). Participants gave written informed consent and received payment. Procedures were approved by the University of California, Riverside Institutional Review Board.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ch4-demographics
#| tbl-cap: "Participant characteristics"
ch3_tbl_demographics(tbl$T1_demographics)
```

### Task, stimuli and sessions {#sec-ch4-2-2}

Participants performed an auditory discrimination task (ADT) and a visual discrimination task (VDT) in the MRI scanner while squeezing a dynamometer with the left hand (@fig-ch4-design, panel A). After a blank gray screen (1.5–4.5 s), a grip gauge appeared for 3 s with a target at 5% (low physical effort) or 40% (high physical effort) of the participant's maximum voluntary contraction (MVC). Participants held the grip until probe offset, when a change in the border color cued them to release it. After a 0.25-s blank and a 0.5-s fixation dot, a standard and a comparison stimulus (the probe; called the target in Chapter 2), each 0.1 s long, were presented 0.5 s apart. In the ADT, the standard was a 1000-Hz tone, and the probe was identical or 8, 16, 32 or 64 Hz higher. In the VDT, the standard was a Gabor patch (1.5 cycles/degree, Michelson contrast 0.20, 4°), and the probe was identical or had a contrast 0.06, 0.12, 0.24 or 0.48 higher. The two smaller offsets were grouped as Hard, the two larger as Easy, and trials with an identical probe as Identical (the catch trials of Chapter 3).

Responses were delayed: participants withheld their response until a cue appeared 0.25 s after probe offset. They then had 3 s to answer "different" (right index finger) or "same" (right middle finger), followed by a confidence rating that is not analyzed here. Each task had five blocks of 30 trials. Each block crossed the five probe levels with the two physical effort levels, three times each, in pseudorandom order. Physical effort was therefore known before each trial, but the stimulus type was known only at probe onset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch4-design
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_design()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F1_design_model.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

The tasks were completed across three sessions on separate days. In Session 1, participants watched instructional videos and practiced at least 60 trials of each task without the grip, and their MVC was measured. They then practiced both tasks with the grip and confidence ratings until the experimenter judged that they understood them. In Sessions 2 and 3, participants performed one task each in the scanner (order counterbalanced), each preceded by a short practice block. MVC was the mean force across three maximal 5-s squeezes, with about 30 s of rest between them. It was measured again in the scanner in Session 2, and that value set the 5% and 40% targets in Sessions 2 and 3.

### Apparatus {#sec-ch4-2-3}

The task ran in Psychophysics Toolbox 3.0.18 [@Brainard1997-fk; @Kleiner2007-fu] in MATLAB R2022b. Visual stimuli were projected with a PROPixx projector (VPixx Technologies; 480 Hz, 1920 × 1080) and viewed through a head-coil mirror (effective viewing distance 12 cm). Sounds were delivered through MRI-compatible earbuds (Newmatic Medical; 30 dB noise reduction). Responses were recorded with a RESPONSEpixx button box, grip force with an MRI-compatible dynamometer (Current Designs; 100 Hz) and pupil diameter with a TRACKPixx binocular eye tracker (VPixx Technologies; 2000 Hz). The background was mid-gray. The gauge's force bar covered less than 1% of the screen, so it changed mean luminance by less than 1% between physical effort levels, in the direction that would constrict the pupil under high physical effort.

### Behavioral data processing {#sec-ch4-2-4}

RT was recorded from the response cue. For modeling it was measured from probe onset, by adding the fixed 0.35-s interval between probe onset and the cue, so that the decision clock starts when evidence becomes available and the non-decision time absorbs the enforced delay. Of `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_raw"))` recorded trials, `r nw(v("n_trials_negative_rt"))` with a negative RT were removed. A further `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_cutoff_excluded"))` with a cue-locked RT below 0.20 s were removed as anticipatory. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_primary"))` trials (@tbl-ch4-trial-counts). Cutoffs of 0.15 s and 0.25 s were used in sensitivity analyses. Overall accuracy was at or below .55 for `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants. They were retained in the primary analysis and excluded in a sensitivity analysis.

### Pupillometry {#sec-ch4-2-5}

Blinks and other artifacts were removed with the ET-remove-artifacts toolbox [@Mather2020-ze] and checked visually. The signal was downsampled to 250 Hz, and each sample was placed on a time axis at 4-ms steps from 3 s before squeeze onset. This axis spans the recorded epoch, which ends with the confidence window 10.7 s after squeeze onset.

The task-evoked pupil response (TEPR) was the mean pupil size 0.3–3.3 s after probe onset (4.65–7.65 s after squeeze onset) minus the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before the probe (3.85–4.35 s, the interstimulus interval). As in Chapter 2, this baseline separates the response to the probe from the slower dilation that builds up during the grip. The window starts 0.3 s after the probe to allow for pupil latency [@Mathot2018-cj] and covers the typical peak, 1–2 s after the stimulus [@da-Silva-Castanheira2021-lq]. Because the window extends past the response on most trials, the TEPR includes post-decision processing; @sec-ch4-2-7 describes how this was tested. Two further measures were the mean pupil size in the 0.5 s before squeeze onset (pre-squeeze baseline) and the mean pupil size during the grip (`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_start"), 2)`–`r fmt_num(v("grip_window_end"), 2)` s), relative to the pre-squeeze baseline.

Trials entered the pupil analyses if at least 50% of samples were valid in both the pre-probe baseline and the TEPR window, and a participant entered a task if at least 20 such trials remained. Of the `r fmt_int(v("n_trials_primary"))` behavioral trials, `r av("pupil_unmatched")` could not be matched to a pupil recording: `r av("pupil_no_flat")` came from `r av("pupil_no_flat_sessions")` sessions of `r av("pupil_no_flat_participants")` participants without a processed recording, and `r av("pupil_unaligned")` came from recorded sessions but could not be aligned to a recorded trial. A further `r av("pupil_axis_refused")` failed the time-axis check. Of the remaining `r av("pupil_after_axis")` trials, `r av("pupil_invalid")` failed the validity criterion (for `r av("pupil_tepr_empty")` of them, the TEPR could not be computed, almost always because the pre-probe baseline from which it is measured had too few valid samples), and `r av("pupil_lt20")` came from participant × task cells with fewer than 20 valid trials. This left `r fmt_int(v("n_pupil_final_trials"))` trials (`r av("pupil_pct_kept")`%) from `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` participants (@fig-ch4-flow). Every participant × task cell contained trials at both physical effort levels, with a median of `r av("cell_median")` trials per level (minimum `r av("cell_min")`), and trials at high physical effort were slightly more likely to be retained (odds ratio = `r av("retain_or")`, 95% CI `r av("retain_ci")`, *p* = `r av("retain_p")`; see "Pupil data" in the Supplementary Materials). Each pupil predictor was centered within participant × task × physical effort and divided by the participant's pooled within-cell SD. Its slope therefore reflects trial-to-trial fluctuation around the condition mean.

### Drift-diffusion model {#sec-ch4-2-6}

Choices and probe-locked RTs were modeled with a Wiener diffusion model [@Ratcliff2008-fj], with "different" as the upper boundary and "same" as the lower boundary (@fig-ch4-design, panel B). Positive drift therefore moves toward "different." The starting point measures a bias toward one response. On Identical trials, drift is negative when evidence accumulates toward the correct "same" response.

Models were fit jointly to both tasks in brms [@Burkner2017-da] with CmdStan [@cmdstan2024], using an identity link for drift, log links for boundary separation (*a*) and non-decision time (*t*~0~), and a logit link for the starting point (*z*). In the primary model (M4), drift depended on stimulus type (Identical, Hard, Easy), task (ADT, VDT), a stimulus type × task interaction, physical effort (low, high) and a physical effort × stimulus term; boundary separation depended on stimulus type, task and physical effort; the starting point depended on task and physical effort; and non-decision time had an intercept only. Identical trials, the ADT and low physical effort were the reference levels. Because the response cue was a fixed delay, non-decision time absorbed that delay, and physical effort effects on it were not tested. Participants had random intercepts on drift, boundary separation and starting point.

The model terms map onto the capacity and policy accounts (@tbl-ch4-predictions). The physical effort main effect on drift shifts drift equally on all trials, toward "different" if positive and toward "same" if negative, a change in the drift criterion [@Ratcliff2008-fj]. The physical effort × stimulus term (stimulus coded +1 for Hard and Easy, −1 for Identical) changes how far drift on trials with a different probe lies from drift on Identical trials, a change in evidence quality. To test whether a loss of evidence quality was largest on the hardest trials, a model in which the physical effort effects varied with task difficulty (M2) was compared with the same model without that interaction (M1). The physical effort effects on boundary separation and on the starting point test the remaining predictions of the policy account. Model selection, robustness variants and formulas are described in the supplement (@sec-ch4-supp-spec).

Priors were weakly informative on the link scale (@tbl-ch4-priors). Models used `r v("n_chains")` chains of `r fmt_int(v("n_iter"))` iterations, the first `r fmt_int(v("n_warmup"))` of them warmup. A model was accepted if every parameter had $\hat{R}$ < 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample sizes of at least 400 and no divergent transitions [@Vehtari2021-bi]. @tbl-ch4-convergence gives the diagnostics for every model.

### Pupil-linked models {#sec-ch4-2-7}

Each pupil-linked model added one pupil predictor to the primary model and was compared with the primary model fit to the same trials. To test which decision component tracked the TEPR, the TEPR was entered on the starting point (P1), on drift with a TEPR × stimulus term (P2) or on boundary separation (P3). To test whether pupil measures taken before the decision predicted boundary separation, the pre-squeeze baseline (P5), the grip-period pupil size (P8) and the previous trial's TEPR within a block (P6) were each entered on boundary separation, and the pre-squeeze baseline was also entered on the starting point (P4). Because the TEPR window overlapped the response, a TEPR–boundary association could reflect decision duration rather than a pupil change before the decision. To test this, P3 was refit without the slowest 20% of trials in each participant × task cell, and pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response was entered on boundary separation (P7).

Physical effort effects on pupil size were tested with paired *t* tests on participant means within each task, with the TEPR compared relative to both the pre-probe and the pre-squeeze baseline. Only participants with valid trials at both physical effort levels were included.

### Statistical inference {#sec-ch4-2-8}

Each effect is summarized by the median of its posterior distribution and a 95% credible interval (CrI), the range that contains the effect with 95% probability given the data and model. We also report the posterior probability that the effect has the sign of its median, for example P(β < 0), which can be read directly as the probability that the effect is negative. To decide whether an effect was negligible rather than merely uncertain, we defined a region of practical equivalence [ROPE, @kruschke2018rejecting], a range of values too small to matter; the more of the posterior that falls inside it, the stronger the evidence that the effect is negligible. The ROPE was ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_a"), 2)` for log boundary separation and logit starting point, about a 5% change in *a* and about 1 percentage point in *z* near its observed value, and ±`r fmt_num(v("rope_v"), 2)` for drift, about 1% of the drift difference between Identical and Easy trials. Bayes factors were not computed because, for effects in a hierarchical diffusion model, they depend strongly on the width of the prior on each effect, and the priors here were weakly informative rather than chosen to represent specific alternative hypotheses [@kruschke2018rejecting].

Models were compared by how well they predicted trials they had not been fitted to, using leave-one-out cross-validation [PSIS-LOO, @Vehtari2017-fy]. The comparison is a difference in expected log predictive density (ΔELPD), which is positive when the model with the added term predicts better. It is reported with its SE, and differences smaller than about twice their SE were treated as uncertain.

Observed accuracy was analyzed with a binomial generalized linear mixed model (stimulus type × physical effort, plus task) in lme4 [@bates2015fitting]. Because models with random physical effort slopes were singular, the model used a random intercept for participant [@Barr2013-maximal; @bates2015parsimonious; @Brauer2018-lmm]. High − Low contrasts at each stimulus type were computed with emmeans [@lenth2024emmeans]. Model adequacy was checked by simulating choices and RTs from the fitted model and comparing them with the observed choice proportions and RT quantiles in each of the 12 task × stimulus type × physical effort cells.

## Results {#sec-ch4-3}

### Primary diffusion model {#sec-ch4-3-1}

**Stimulus and task effects.** Because "different" was the upper boundary, positive drift favors "different" and negative drift favors "same." Observed accuracy was `r av("acc_ident")`% on Identical trials, `r av("acc_easy")`% on Easy trials and `r av("acc_hard")`% on Hard trials (@fig-ch4-accuracy). Drift was negative on Identical and Hard trials and positive on Easy trials (@fig-ch4-condition-params; @tbl-ch4-condition-cells), so that on Hard trials evidence on average favored "same" although the probe differed (low physical effort; ADT: `r cell_s("v_cell_ADT_Hard")`; VDT: `r cell_s("v_cell_VDT_Hard")`). In both tasks the starting point lay above 0.5, toward the "different" boundary (ADT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_ADT")`; VDT: *z* = `r prob_s("z_VDT")`). Differences between stimulus types and tasks in drift and boundary separation are given in @tbl-ch4-fixef-m4.


```{r}
#| label: fig-ch4-condition-params
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_condition_params()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F2_condition_parameters.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

**Physical effort effects.** High physical effort shifted drift toward "same" on all trials (drift criterion: `r eff("crit")`; @fig-ch4-effort-forest; @tbl-ch4-effort-effects). The physical effort × stimulus term, which indexes evidence quality, was close to zero (`r eff("qual")`). Drift decreased on trials with a different probe (`r eff("drift_diff_trials")`); on Identical trials the change was smaller, and its interval included zero (`r eff("drift_same_trials")`). Allowing the physical effort effects on drift and boundary separation to vary with task difficulty did not improve prediction (`r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`; @tbl-ch4-model-comparison). In that model, the physical effort effect on drift was more negative on Hard than on Easy trials (Hard − Easy: `r eff("m2_v_hard_minus_easy_x_high")`), whereas the corresponding contrast on boundary separation included zero (`r eff("m2_bs_hard_minus_easy_x_high")`; @tbl-ch4-m2-interactions). Under high physical effort, boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("bs")`, with the whole posterior inside the ROPE (`r fmt_rope("bs")`), and the starting point did not change (`r eff("bias", rope = TRUE)`).

In a mixed model of accuracy, high physical effort lowered accuracy on Hard trials (High − Low: `r acc_s("acc_high_low_Hard")`), raised it slightly, but not significantly, on Identical trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Standard")`) and left it unchanged on Easy trials (`r acc_s("acc_high_low_Easy")`; @tbl-ch4-acc-contrasts). The observed means showed the same pattern: accuracy was `r sub("^[−-]", "", av("acc_hard_diff"))` percentage points lower on Hard trials and `r av("acc_ident_diff")` percentage points higher on Identical trials under high physical effort (@fig-ch4-accuracy).

### Robustness of the physical effort effects {#sec-ch4-3-2}

The drift criterion shift was unchanged when the physical effort effects were allowed to vary across participants (M4r: `r eff("crit_M4r")`). The between-participant SD of that effect was small (`r est_s("sd_effort_M4r")`). The shift was also stable at RT cutoffs of 0.15 s (`r eff("crit_thr015")`) and 0.25 s (`r eff("crit_thr025")`). Excluding the `r v("n_subchance_excluded")` participants with near-chance accuracy left the point estimate unchanged. With *N* = `r v("n_subchance_remaining")`, however, the interval included zero (`r eff("crit_subchance")`). When physical effort effects were allowed to differ by task (M4b), the criterion shift was larger in the ADT (`r eff("crit_ADT_M4b")`) than in the VDT (`r eff("crit_VDT_M4b")`), but the task difference was uncertain (`r eff("m4b_effort_x_task")`). The evidence-quality term was close to zero in every variant. The boundary effect was positive at the 0.25-s cutoff (`r eff("bs_thr025", pct = TRUE)`) and after the near-chance exclusion (`r eff("bs_subchance", pct = TRUE)`), but at the 0.15-s cutoff its interval included zero (`r eff("bs_thr015", pct = TRUE)`; @tbl-ch4-robustness).

### Pupil-linked decision dynamics {#sec-ch4-3-3}

**Physical effort and pupil size.** High physical effort increased pupil size during the grip (1.00–4.35 s after squeeze onset, relative to the 0.5 s before squeeze onset) in the ADT (`r pt_s("grip_high_low_ADT")`), and the difference was not reliable in the VDT (`r pt_s("grip_high_low_VDT")`). Relative to the pre-probe baseline, the TEPR was smaller under high physical effort in both tasks (ADT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B1")`; VDT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B1")`). Relative to the pre-squeeze baseline, it did not differ between physical effort levels (ADT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_ADT_B0")`; VDT: `r pt_s("tepr_high_low_VDT_B0")`; @tbl-ch4-pupil-descriptives; @fig-ch4-pupil-timecourse; @fig-ch4-grip-participants). These pupil comparisons were unchanged when only participants with at least 10 trials at each physical effort level were included or when trials rather than participant means were analyzed; equalizing trial counts between physical effort levels by subsampling weakened the two smaller effects (@tbl-ch4-pupil-sensitivity). In the pupil sample, boundary separation was wider under high physical effort (`r eff("P0_bs", pct = TRUE)`), and the drift criterion shift had the same sign as in the full sample, with an interval that included zero (`r eff("P0_crit")`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ch4-pupil-timecourse
#| fig-cap: !expr cap_fig_pupil_timecourse()
#| out-width: "100%"
suppressWarnings(knitr::include_graphics(normalizePath(file.path(params$figures_dir, "F4_pupil_timecourse.png"), mustWork = TRUE), error = FALSE))
```

**Pupil predictors of decision parameters.** Boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("P3_bs")` per within-person SD of the TEPR, and adding the TEPR improved out-of-sample prediction (`r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3_vs_P0")`; @fig-ch4-pupil-boundary; @tbl-ch4-pupil-ordering). TEPR did not predict the starting point (`r eff("P1_bias")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P1_vs_P0")`) or drift (TEPR: `r eff("P2_drift_tepr")`; TEPR × stimulus: `r eff("P2_drift_tepr_x_stim")`; `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P2_vs_P0")`; @tbl-ch4-pupil-models).

**Timing of the TEPR–boundary association.** TEPR correlated with RT within participants (`r fmt_r(v("tepr_rt_r", "r"), v("tepr_rt_r", "lo"), v("tepr_rt_r", "hi"))`). After the slowest 20% of trials in each participant and task were removed, boundary separation changed by `r pct_s("P3_rt_bs")` per SD of the TEPR, and the predictive gain was less than twice its standard error (`r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P3rt_vs_P0rt")`). Pupil size in the 0.5 s before the response was associated with wider boundaries and improved prediction (`r pct_s("P7_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P7_vs_P0pre")`). The measures taken before the decision did not predict boundary separation: previous-trial TEPR (`r pct_s("P6_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P6_vs_P0lag")`), pre-squeeze baseline pupil (`r pct_s("P5_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P5_vs_P0base")`) and grip-period pupil (`r pct_s("P8_bs")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P8_vs_P0grip")`). The pre-squeeze baseline did not predict the starting point either (`r eff("P4_bias_base")`, `r fmt_elpd("delta_elpd_P4_vs_P0base")`).

### Model adequacy {#sec-ch4-3-4}

The primary model reproduced the observed choice proportions in `r v("ppc_choice_inside_M4")` of 12 condition cells (@tbl-ch4-ppc-choice). Of the observed RT quantiles, `r fmt_num(v("ppc_rt_inside_pct_M4"), 1)`% fell inside the 95% predictive intervals, and observed median RTs were on average `r fmt_int(v("ppc_rt_median_bias_ms_M4"))` ms slower than predicted (@fig-ch4-ppc). The discrepancy was largest for minority responses ("different" on Identical trials, "same" on Easy trials and "different" on Hard trials), which were slower than predicted. After moment matching and exact refits (@sec-ch4-supp-spec), no observation in any compared model had a Pareto *k* above 0.7. Non-decision time changed with the RT cutoff: `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr015", "median"), 3)` s, `r fmt_num(v("t0_M4", "median"), 3)` s and `r fmt_num(v("t0_thr025", "median"), 3)` s at cutoffs of 0.15 s, 0.20 s and 0.25 s.

## Discussion {#sec-ch4-4}

@tbl-ch4-predictions set out what the capacity and policy accounts predict. On the predictions that separate them, the results favored the policy account, with one qualification discussed in @sec-ch4-disc-capacity. The physical effort × stimulus term, which measures evidence quality, was close to zero. High physical effort instead shifted drift toward "same" on all trials, a change in the drift criterion. Accuracy fell on Hard trials, as both accounts predict, and on Identical trials it rose slightly rather than falling, as a criterion shift toward "same" predicts and a loss of evidence quality does not, although that gain was not significant (compare @fig-ch4-accuracy with @fig-ch4-predictions, panel B). Boundary separation changed by a practically negligible amount, and the starting point did not change. High physical effort enlarged the pupil only weakly during the grip, reliably in the ADT alone. In the pupil sample, trials with larger pupil responses during the decision had wider boundaries, whereas no pupil measure taken before the decision predicted boundary separation.

### Evidence quality and the capacity account {#sec-ch4-disc-capacity}

The capacity account made two predictions: high physical effort should reduce evidence quality, and this loss should be largest on the hardest trials [@Kahneman1973-jw; @Wickens2008-pj]. The physical effort × stimulus term, which measures evidence quality, was close to zero, and its interval allowed a small decline but not a large one. In the model that let the physical effort effects vary with task difficulty, physical effort lowered drift more on Hard than on Easy trials, but that contrast only just excluded zero, and the model did not predict better than the model without the interaction (`r elpd_s("delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1", "se_delta_elpd_M2_vs_M1")`; @tbl-ch4-model-comparison; @tbl-ch4-m2-interactions). The data therefore leave room for a small capacity cost on the hardest discriminations, in addition to the criterion shift.

The main physical effort effect was a shift common to all trials. In diffusion-model terms, this is a change in the drift criterion: the reference point against which evidence is evaluated as favoring one response or the other [@Ratcliff2008-fj]. Because the upper boundary was "different," the criterion shift lowers drift on trials with a different probe, so those trials more often end in "same." On Identical trials the same shift moves drift further toward the correct response. The accuracy pattern follows from this. The Hard-trial cost is the change that a capacity account would predict, but here it arises mainly from a change in the criterion rather than a loss of evidence quality. Accuracy alone cannot separate the two, because Hard trials were the trials on which the shift was most consequential.

### The criterion shift {#sec-ch4-4-2}

The earlier chapters point to the same conclusion: high physical effort did not take capacity away from the judgment. In younger adults, task difficulty and physical effort did not interact on any measure [Chapter 2, @Dastgheib2026-crpi], and in the present sample, psychometric functions showed that high physical effort lowered "different" responses without reducing sensitivity. The reduction on Identical trials was similar in size but uncertain on its own (Chapter 3). The diffusion model places that shift in the drift criterion and adds the hint of a small additional cost on the hardest trials, which Chapter 2 did not detect. Because this chapter has no younger comparison group, and Chapter 2 used a laboratory setting and different stimulus offsets, the data cannot show whether that cost is specific to older adults.

Within the policy account, wider boundaries under high physical effort would indicate that participants protected accuracy, and narrower boundaries that they ended effortful trials sooner. Neither occurred: the estimated change was positive but practically negligible, and its interval included zero at the shortest RT cutoff. The starting point was also unchanged, so physical effort did not bias either response before the stimulus appeared. The results therefore fit the policy account, but through the drift criterion rather than through boundary separation or the starting point.

Why high physical effort would shift the criterion is not settled by these data. Chapter 3 considers three explanations: a more conservative decision policy under a concurrent demand, a change in decision processing linked to the pupil, and a bias tied to the finger used for each response. The pupil results (@sec-ch4-4-4) do not support the second, because no pupil measure taken before the decision predicted the decision parameters. The response mapping (@sec-ch4-4-5) leaves the third open.

### Physical effort and pupil size {#sec-ch4-4-3}

High physical effort increased pupil size during the grip in the ADT, as expected from the pupil's sensitivity to physical effort [@Zenon2014-ze]; in the VDT the difference had the same sign but was not reliable. When both tasks were analyzed together with participant-specific physical effort effects (Chapter 3), the grip-period difference was not reliable, so the effect of physical effort on pupil size during the grip was weak. After the probe, the pupil rose less under high physical effort from its level before the probe, but pupil size after the probe, measured from before the squeeze, did not differ between physical effort levels. The smaller response under high physical effort therefore reflects the higher level from which the pupil rose, not a smaller pupil after the probe, which is why the choice of baseline matters for physical effort comparisons [@Mathot2018-cj]. The release of the grip, and the color change that cued it, also fall inside the TEPR window, and releasing a grip held at high physical effort differs from releasing one held at low physical effort.

One interpretation of pupil changes with physical effort comes from adaptive gain theory, which links pupil size to activity of the locus coeruleus–noradrenaline system [@Aston-Jones2005-dg; @Joshi2016-zb]. Isometric handgrip engages this system [@Mather2020-ze], and the locus coeruleus is vulnerable in aging [@Mather2016-bx]. This study did not manipulate locus coeruleus activity, and the neuroimaging measures of that activity are not analyzed here. Pupil size also covaries with activity outside the locus coeruleus [@Joshi2016-zb].

### Pupil size and boundary separation {#sec-ch4-4-4}

Of the pupil measures, trial-wise TEPR had the strongest association with boundary separation, which parallels work in which larger pupil dilation on high-conflict choices predicted wider boundaries [@Cavanagh2014-eh]. Two results limit how far this association can be read as evidence that pupil-linked arousal made participants more cautious on that trial. First, the TEPR window overlapped the response, TEPR correlated with RT within participants, and when the slowest trials were removed the association was about half as large and its predictive gain was no longer clearly above its standard error. A wider boundary lengthens the decision, and a longer decision lets more of the pupil response accumulate in the window. Second, none of the measures taken before the decision (the pre-squeeze baseline, the grip-period pupil and the previous trial's TEPR) predicted boundary separation.

Pupil size in the 0.5 s just before the response was also larger on trials with wider boundaries, so the association does not arise only from processing after the response. This measure still cannot show that arousal made participants more cautious. Because the window was defined relative to the response, it captured a later stage of the pupil response on slower trials, and wider boundaries make trials slower. A larger value would therefore be expected on those trials even if the pupil played no part in setting the boundary. Only a measure taken before the decision begins can test that influence, and none of those measures predicted boundary separation. Pupil size therefore tracked the decision as it unfolded, not a state that preceded it. Separating the two would require a window fixed to probe onset that ends before the earliest response, but in this design the 0.35 s between probe onset and the response cue is too short for the pupil response to develop [@Mathot2018-cj].

### Limitations and future directions {#sec-ch4-4-5}

**Boundary terms.** Boundary separation was allowed to vary with stimulus type, although stimulus types were intermixed and could not be anticipated. These terms let the model absorb RT differences between stimulus types that a diffusion model without across-trial variability cannot otherwise capture. This was most evident for minority responses, which were slower than predicted. That slow-error pattern is the signature of variability in drift across trials [@Ratcliff2008-fj]. The physical effort contrasts were stable across model variants and RT cutoffs, but absolute parameter values depend on this choice. Models with across-trial variability in drift and non-decision time [@ratcliff2002estimating] would test whether the physical effort effects survive a better account of RT distributions.

**Delayed-response design.** Because participants waited for a cue, non-decision time absorbed the enforced delay and changed almost one-for-one with the RT cutoff. It cannot be interpreted as encoding or motor time, and physical effort effects on it were not tested. The design also limits how much RT information constrains boundary separation. A free-response version of the task would test the boundary results more directly.

**Pupil sample and measure.** The pupil analyses used `r v("n_pupil_final_subjects")` of the `r v("n_final")` participants and `r av("pupil_pct_kept")`% of the trials, selected on recording quality, and they are correlational at the level of trials. In that sample, the physical effort effects on the drift criterion and boundary separation had the same sign as in the full sample. The TEPR window included post-decision processing. In addition, the pre-probe baseline began shortly after the standard and so included the onset of the pupil response to it; the TEPR therefore measures the response to the probe on top of a still-rising response to the standard. The grip-period measure combined dilation related to physical effort with trial-to-trial variation in the force produced. Entering the recorded trial-wise grip force as a covariate would separate the two.

**Design.** With only two levels of physical effort, the study cannot test non-monotonic effects. Hard trials were answered incorrectly more often than correctly, so Hard-trial estimates reflect a strong bias toward "same" as well as low evidence quality. When participants with near-chance accuracy were excluded, the criterion shift kept its size, but its interval included zero. The effect is small and should be replicated.

**Response mapping.** "Different" was always given with the right index finger and "same" with the right middle finger, while the left hand held the grip. A bias acting on the evidence for one response therefore cannot be separated from the finger that gave that response; counterbalancing the mapping across participants would separate them.

**Physiological measures.** Pupil size is the only physiological measure reported here. Neuroimaging was collected during the task, including locus coeruleus activity, but those measures are outside the scope of this dissertation. Links between the pupil results and the noradrenergic system therefore remain interpretive.

**Setting.** Data were collected in an MRI scanner, which constrains luminance, posture and noise, so pupil responses and grip performance may differ from those in a laboratory.

### Conclusion {#sec-ch4-4-6}

In older adults, holding a 40% MVC grip during an auditory or visual same–different judgment shifted the drift criterion toward "same." It did not reduce the overall quality of the evidence accumulated or meaningfully change boundary separation. Pupil responses during the decision were larger on trials with wider boundaries, but pupil size measured before the decision did not predict boundary separation. In behavior, high physical effort made older adults less likely to report a difference, an accuracy cost that fell on the small differences that are hardest to detect.
